claim: The dynamics of host-parasite interactions are highly temperature-dependent.
source: The dynamics of host-parasite interactions are highly temperature-dependent and may be modified by increasing frequency and intensity of climate-driven heat events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, representing a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Diurnal fluctuations of ±3°C lowered infection rates compared to constant temperatures in Daphnia magna exposed to Ordospora colligata.
source: We found that diurnal fluctuations of ±3°C lowered infection rates and reduced spore burden compared to constant temperatures in our focal host Daphnia magna exposed to the microsporidium parasite Ordospora colligata.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Diurnal fluctuations of ±3°C reduced spore burden compared to constant temperatures in Daphnia magna exposed to Ordospora colligata.
source: We found that diurnal fluctuations of ±3°C lowered infection rates and reduced spore burden compared to constant temperatures in our focal host Daphnia magna exposed to the microsporidium parasite Ordospora colligata.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: A 3-day heatwave (+6°C) did not affect infection rates relative to constant temperatures with the same mean.
source: In contrast, a 3-day heatwave (+6°C) did not affect infection rates, but increased spore burden (relative to constant temperatures with the same mean) at 16°C, while reducing burden at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: A 3-day heatwave (+6°C) increased spore burden at 16°C relative to constant temperatures with the same mean.
source: In contrast, a 3-day heatwave (+6°C) did not affect infection rates, but increased spore burden (relative to constant temperatures with the same mean) at 16°C, while reducing burden at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: A 3-day heatwave (+6°C) reduced spore burden at higher temperatures relative to constant temperatures with the same mean.
source: In contrast, a 3-day heatwave (+6°C) did not affect infection rates, but increased spore burden (relative to constant temperatures with the same mean) at 16°C, while reducing burden at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Infectious diseases have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on human populations.
source: One of the major challenges of the 21st century is understanding how infectious diseases, which have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on human (Hotez et al., 2014), agricultural (Chakraborty and Newton, 2011), and wildlife (Harvell et al., 2019) populations, will be affected by climate change.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hotez et al., 2014.

claim: Infectious diseases have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on agricultural populations.
source: One of the major challenges of the 21st century is understanding how infectious diseases, which have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on human (Hotez et al., 2014), agricultural (Chakraborty and Newton, 2011), and wildlife (Harvell et al., 2019) populations, will be affected by climate change.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chakraborty and Newton, 2011.

claim: Infectious diseases have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on wildlife populations.
source: One of the major challenges of the 21st century is understanding how infectious diseases, which have profound ecological and epidemiological impacts on human (Hotez et al., 2014), agricultural (Chakraborty and Newton, 2011), and wildlife (Harvell et al., 2019) populations, will be affected by climate change.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harvell et al., 2019.

claim: The interaction between hosts and their pathogens is sensitive to temperature.
source: It is now well-established that the interaction between hosts and their pathogens is sensitive to temperature (Kirk et al., 2020; Rohr et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirk et al., 2020 and Rohr et al., 2013.

claim: Disease transmission can increase with temperature.
source: For example, disease transmission (Ben-Horin et al., 2013), host immunity (Dittmar et al., 2014; Rohr and Raffel, 2010), and pathogen growth (Gehman et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2018) can increase with temperature, while other host-pathogen life-history traits such as lifespan and fecundity can decrease (Altizer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ben-Horin et al., 2013.

claim: Host immunity can increase with temperature.
source: For example, disease transmission (Ben-Horin et al., 2013), host immunity (Dittmar et al., 2014; Rohr and Raffel, 2010), and pathogen growth (Gehman et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2018) can increase with temperature, while other host-pathogen life-history traits such as lifespan and fecundity can decrease (Altizer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dittmar et al., 2014 and Rohr and Raffel, 2010.

claim: Pathogen growth can increase with temperature.
source: For example, disease transmission (Ben-Horin et al., 2013), host immunity (Dittmar et al., 2014; Rohr and Raffel, 2010), and pathogen growth (Gehman et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2018) can increase with temperature, while other host-pathogen life-history traits such as lifespan and fecundity can decrease (Altizer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gehman et al., 2018 and Kirk et al., 2018.

claim: Host-pathogen life-history traits such as lifespan and fecundity can decrease with temperature.
source: For example, disease transmission (Ben-Horin et al., 2013), host immunity (Dittmar et al., 2014; Rohr and Raffel, 2010), and pathogen growth (Gehman et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2018) can increase with temperature, while other host-pathogen life-history traits such as lifespan and fecundity can decrease (Altizer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Altizer et al., 2013.

claim: Climate change is predicted to increase mean temperatures.
source: Climate change is predicted to increase not only mean temperatures, but also temperature fluctuations and the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events (Schär et al., 2004; Vasseur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schär et al., 2004 and Vasseur et al., 2014.

claim: Climate change is predicted to increase temperature fluctuations.
source: Climate change is predicted to increase not only mean temperatures, but also temperature fluctuations and the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events (Schär et al., 2004; Vasseur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schär et al., 2004 and Vasseur et al., 2014.

claim: Climate change is predicted to increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events.
source: Climate change is predicted to increase not only mean temperatures, but also temperature fluctuations and the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events (Schär et al., 2004; Vasseur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schär et al., 2004 and Vasseur et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in temperature variance have the potential to modify host-pathogen dynamics.
source: Such changes in temperature variance have the potential to modify host-pathogen dynamics (Franke et al., 2019; Rohr et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Franke et al., 2019 and Rohr et al., 2013.

claim: Diurnal temperature fluctuations have been shown to increase malaria transmission at the lower end of the thermal range.
source: For instance, diurnal temperature fluctuations have been shown to increase malaria transmission at the lower end of the thermal range (Paaijmans et al., 2010), while short-term temperature fluctuations led to reduced transmission success due to lower filtration rates in a Daphnia-pathogen system (Dallas and Drake, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paaijmans et al., 2010.

claim: Short-term temperature fluctuations led to reduced transmission success due to lower filtration rates in a Daphnia-pathogen system.
source: For instance, diurnal temperature fluctuations have been shown to increase malaria transmission at the lower end of the thermal range (Paaijmans et al., 2010), while short-term temperature fluctuations led to reduced transmission success due to lower filtration rates in a Daphnia-pathogen system (Dallas and Drake, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dallas and Drake, 2016.

claim: The effect of extreme heat events on host and pathogen traits may depend on the magnitude, duration, and intensity of the applied heatwave.
source: The effect of extreme heat events on host and pathogen traits is also highly variable and may depend on the magnitude, duration, and intensity of the applied heatwave (Landis et al., 2012; Schreven et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Landis et al., 2012, Schreven et al., 2017, and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: In a parasitoid-insect interaction, a heatwave of 5°C resulted in greater parasitoid development.
source: In a parasitoid-insect interaction, a heatwave of 5°C resulted in greater parasitoid development while a 10°C increase reduced parasitoid growth (Schreven et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schreven et al., 2017.

claim: In a parasitoid-insect interaction, a 10°C increase reduced parasitoid growth.
source: In a parasitoid-insect interaction, a heatwave of 5°C resulted in greater parasitoid development while a 10°C increase reduced parasitoid growth (Schreven et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schreven et al., 2017.

claim: Daphnia are a well-established ecological model system.
source: Daphnia are a well-established ecological model system (Miner et al., 2012) used frequently in climate change studies (e.g., Dallas and Drake, 2016; Hector et al., 2019; Kirk et al., 2020), while Ordospora transmission is representative of a classical environmentally transmitted pathogen (i.e., it mimics diseases such as SARS-CoV-2 and Vibrio cholerae) and meets the assumptions of conventional epidemiological models (e.g., infection following mass action [Kirk et al., 2019], continuous shedding of infectious particles [Ebert, 2005] and little or no spatial structure within host populations).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miner et al., 2012.

claim: Daphnia are used frequently in climate change studies.
source: Daphnia are a well-established ecological model system (Miner et al., 2012) used frequently in climate change studies (e.g., Dallas and Drake, 2016; Hector et al., 2019; Kirk et al., 2020), while Ordospora transmission is representative of a classical environmentally transmitted pathogen (i.e., it mimics diseases such as SARS-CoV-2 and Vibrio cholerae) and meets the assumptions of conventional epidemiological models (e.g., infection following mass action [Kirk et al., 2019], continuous shedding of infectious particles [Ebert, 2005] and little or no spatial structure within host populations).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dallas and Drake, 2016, Hector et al., 2019, and Kirk et al., 2020.

claim: Ordospora transmission is representative of a classical environmentally transmitted pathogen.
source: Daphnia are a well-established ecological model system (Miner et al., 2012) used frequently in climate change studies (e.g., Dallas and Drake, 2016; Hector et al., 2019; Kirk et al., 2020), while Ordospora transmission is representative of a classical environmentally transmitted pathogen (i.e., it mimics diseases such as SARS-CoV-2 and Vibrio cholerae) and meets the assumptions of conventional epidemiological models (e.g., infection following mass action [Kirk et al., 2019], continuous shedding of infectious particles [Ebert, 2005] and little or no spatial structure within host populations).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statement that Ordospora mimics diseases such as SARS-CoV-2 and Vibrio cholerae, and by citations to Kirk et al., 2019 and Ebert, 2005.

claim: Ordospora meets the assumptions of conventional epidemiological models.
source: Daphnia are a well-established ecological model system (Miner et al., 2012) used frequently in climate change studies (e.g., Dallas and Drake, 2016; Hector et al., 2019; Kirk et al., 2020), while Ordospora transmission is representative of a classical environmentally transmitted pathogen (i.e., it mimics diseases such as SARS-CoV-2 and Vibrio cholerae) and meets the assumptions of conventional epidemiological models (e.g., infection following mass action [Kirk et al., 2019], continuous shedding of infectious particles [Ebert, 2005] and little or no spatial structure within host populations).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirk et al., 2019 and Ebert, 2005.

claim: The experimental design comprised seven constant temperature regimes with temperatures ranging from 10°C to 28°C.
source: Our experimental design comprised seven constant temperature regimes with temperatures ranging from 10°C to 28°C, five variable temperature regimes mimicking diurnal temperature fluctuations of ±3°C around the mean, and four heatwave regimes where temperatures were identical to the equivalent constant treatment except during a 3-day period between days 20 and 23 when temperatures were raised by 6°C.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The experimental design comprised five variable temperature regimes mimicking diurnal temperature fluctuations of ±3°C around the mean.
source: Our experimental design comprised seven constant temperature regimes with temperatures ranging from 10°C to 28°C, five variable temperature regimes mimicking diurnal temperature fluctuations of ±3°C around the mean, and four heatwave regimes where temperatures were identical to the equivalent constant treatment except during a 3-day period between days 20 and 23 when temperatures were raised by 6°C.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The experimental design comprised four heatwave regimes where temperatures were identical to the equivalent constant treatment except during a 3-day period between days 20 and 23 when temperatures were raised by 6°C.
source: Our experimental design comprised seven constant temperature regimes with temperatures ranging from 10°C to 28°C, five variable temperature regimes mimicking diurnal temperature fluctuations of ±3°C around the mean, and four heatwave regimes where temperatures were identical to the equivalent constant treatment except during a 3-day period between days 20 and 23 when temperatures were raised by 6°C.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Diurnal temperature fluctuations narrowed the thermal performance curve for infectivity compared with constant temperatures.
source: Diurnal temperature fluctuations narrowed the thermal performance curve for infectivity compared with constant temperatures (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The estimated maximum temperature at which spores were able to cause infections was 5°C lower under fluctuating temperatures than under constant temperatures.
source: The estimated (using the Beta Function) maximum temperature at which spores were able to cause infections was 5°C lower under fluctuating temperatures than under constant temperatures (Figure 2A; Tmax=25°C for fluctuating vs. 30°C for constant; confidence intervals for Tmax do not overlap).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The thermal performance curve for infectivity under the heatwave was almost identical to that under constant temperature.
source: The thermal performance curve for infectivity under the heatwave, where temperatures were raised by 6°C for 3 days and then returned to constant temperature (Figure 1), was almost identical to that under constant temperature (all confidence intervals overlap, Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The highest rate of infection occurred at 19°C.
source: Remaining parameter estimates of the Beta Function were similar for the three temperature regimes, with the highest rate of infection at 19°C, a maximum infection rate of ~95% infection and no infections under 10°C (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2; confidence intervals overlap for Topt, Fm, and Tmin).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The maximum infection rate was approximately 95%.
source: Remaining parameter estimates of the Beta Function were similar for the three temperature regimes, with the highest rate of infection at 19°C, a maximum infection rate of ~95% infection and no infections under 10°C (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2; confidence intervals overlap for Topt, Fm, and Tmin).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No infections occurred under 10°C.
source: Remaining parameter estimates of the Beta Function were similar for the three temperature regimes, with the highest rate of infection at 19°C, a maximum infection rate of ~95% infection and no infections under 10°C (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2; confidence intervals overlap for Topt, Fm, and Tmin).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Daily temperature fluctuation led to a lower maximum temperature (by ~3°C) for parasite growth within the host.
source: Consistent with infection rates, daily temperature fluctuation led to a lower maximum temperature (by ~3°C) for parasite growth within the host, resulting in a narrowed thermal performance curve for burden compared with the other temperature regimes (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 3, non-overlapping confidence intervals for Tmax).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spore burden in the heatwave showed a shift in the optimum temperature from 19.4°C to 15.7°C compared to the constant temperature regime.
source: Compared to the constant temperature regime, spore burden in the heatwave showed a shift in the optimum temperature (from 19.4°C to 15.7°C), and an increase in the number of spore clusters (Figure 2B, confidence intervals for Topt and Fm do not overlap).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spore burden in the heatwave showed an increase in the number of spore clusters compared to the constant temperature regime.
source: Compared to the constant temperature regime, spore burden in the heatwave showed a shift in the optimum temperature (from 19.4°C to 15.7°C), and an increase in the number of spore clusters (Figure 2B, confidence intervals for Topt and Fm do not overlap).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spore burden at 16°C differed by almost an order of magnitude between diurnal fluctuations and heatwave (86 vs. 737 spore clusters).
source: Moreover, due to the opposite effects at 16°C for both variable temperature regimes (i.e., a narrowing of performance under fluctuating temperatures, exacerbation under heatwave), spore burden at this temperature differed by almost an order of magnitude (i.e., 86 vs. 737 spore clusters).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Daphnia exposed to the parasite had lower reproductive success near the optimum temperature (~20°C) compared to control animals that were not exposed to Ordospora.
source: Daphnia exposed to the parasite had lower reproductive success near the optimum temperature (~20°C) compared to control animals that were not exposed to Ordospora (non-overlapping confidence intervals for Fm) and lost between 8% (constant) and 24% (diurnal fluctuation) of reproductive output (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Daphnia exposed to Ordospora lost between 8% (constant) and 24% (diurnal fluctuation) of reproductive output.
source: Daphnia exposed to the parasite had lower reproductive success near the optimum temperature (~20°C) compared to control animals that were not exposed to Ordospora (non-overlapping confidence intervals for Fm) and lost between 8% (constant) and 24% (diurnal fluctuation) of reproductive output (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Animals exposed to Ordospora in variable temperatures had lower reproductive success.
source: Comparing host performance among the different temperature regimes shows that animals exposed to Ordospora in variable temperatures had lower reproductive success (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for Fm), with a small shift (1.1°C) in their thermal optimum under the heatwave regime (Figure 2C, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for Topt).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Animals exposed to Ordospora showed a small shift (1.1°C) in their thermal optimum under the heatwave regime.
source: Comparing host performance among the different temperature regimes shows that animals exposed to Ordospora in variable temperatures had lower reproductive success (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for Fm), with a small shift (1.1°C) in their thermal optimum under the heatwave regime (Figure 2C, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for Topt).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Control animals that were not exposed to Ordospora had lower fitness after the heatwave.
source: Control animals that were not exposed to Ordospora also had lower fitness after the heatwave (Figure 3, non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for Fm) and, while reproduction at the optimal temperature of the control animals experiencing diurnal fluctuations was lower, confidence intervals overlapped with the constant temperature regime (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Daphnia, filtration rates determine the contact rate between host and pathogen.
source: In Daphnia, filtration rates determine the contact rate between host and pathogen, and a reduction in filtration can thus lead to reduced levels of infection (Hall et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2010.

claim: A reduction in filtration can lead to reduced levels of infection in Daphnia.
source: In Daphnia, filtration rates determine the contact rate between host and pathogen, and a reduction in filtration can thus lead to reduced levels of infection (Hall et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2010.

claim: Filtration rates of D. magna decline at higher temperatures.
source: As filtration rates of D. magna decline at higher temperatures (Kirk et al., 2019), average infection rates under diurnal temperature fluctuations would also be expected to be lower due to the non-linear nature of the thermal performance curve (i.e., Jensen's inequality; Dowd et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2019.

claim: Infection probability in the Daphnia-Ordospora system decreases sharply when temperatures surpass 22°C.
source: In addition, infection probability in our study system decreases sharply when temperatures surpass 22°C (Kirk et al., 2019), reducing infection rates under fluctuating temperatures that exceed this temperature (again, due to Jensen's inequality).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2019.

claim: Daphnia are not known to recover from Ordospora infection.
source: However, given that our heatwave occurred 20 days post-infection and that Daphnia are not known to recover from infection (Ebert, 2005), the effect of the heatwave on established infections may have been limited.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert, 2005.

claim: Absence of an effect of a heatwave on infection rates has been found for a pipefish-trematode host-parasite system.
source: Absence of an effect of a heatwave on infection rates has also been found for a pipefish-trematode host-parasite system (Landis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Landis et al., 2012.

claim: Multiple studies suggest a shift in the thermal performance of parasite fitness under fluctuating temperatures.
source: The impact of diurnal temperature fluctuations on parasite fitness has been studied previously, with multiple studies suggesting a shift in the thermal performance of parasite fitness under fluctuating temperatures (Dallas and Drake, 2016; Duncan et al., 2011; Greenspan et al., 2017a; Paaijmans et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dallas and Drake, 2016, Duncan et al., 2011, Greenspan et al., 2017a, and Paaijmans et al., 2010.

claim: Estimates and predictions that ignore temperature variation may over- or underestimate disease burden and prevalence.
source: Indeed, our findings that Ordospora has a narrower thermal performance for spore burden and infectivity under fluctuating temperatures adds to a growing body of evidence (Dallas and Drake, 2016; Greenspan et al., 2017b; Hector et al., 2019; Roth et al., 2010) suggesting that estimates and predictions that ignore temperature variation may over- or underestimate disease burden and prevalence (Greenspan et al., 2017a; Raffel et al., 2012; Rohr et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dallas and Drake, 2016, Greenspan et al., 2017b, Hector et al., 2019, Roth et al., 2010, Greenspan et al., 2017a, Raffel et al., 2012, and Rohr et al., 2013.

claim: In a fish-tapeworm host-parasite system, parasite growth, egg production, and the number of first-stage larvae increased after a 1-week exposure to higher temperatures (increase up to 7.5°C).
source: It was shown recently in a fish-tapeworm host-parasite system that parasite growth, egg production, and the number of first-stage larvae increased after a 1-week exposure to higher temperatures (increase up to 7.5°C) (Franke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Franke et al., 2019.

claim: Some studies have reported increased disease susceptibility following heatwaves.
source: Although some studies have reported increased disease susceptibility following heatwaves (Dittmar et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2010), others found no effect on immune function (Stahlschmidt et al., 2017) or reduced disease performance after exposure to high temperatures (Fayer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dittmar et al., 2014 and Roth et al., 2010.

claim: Some studies found no effect of heatwaves on immune function.
source: Although some studies have reported increased disease susceptibility following heatwaves (Dittmar et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2010), others found no effect on immune function (Stahlschmidt et al., 2017) or reduced disease performance after exposure to high temperatures (Fayer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stahlschmidt et al., 2017.

claim: Some studies found reduced disease performance after exposure to high temperatures.
source: Although some studies have reported increased disease susceptibility following heatwaves (Dittmar et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2010), others found no effect on immune function (Stahlschmidt et al., 2017) or reduced disease performance after exposure to high temperatures (Fayer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fayer et al., 1998.

claim: The effect of a heatwave on parasite traits depends on the amplitude of the extreme event in plant-endoparasite and herbivore-parasitoid systems.
source: This context-dependency of heatwaves is supported further by studies in both plant-endoparasite (Schreven et al., 2017) and herbivore-parasitoid (Zhang et al., 2019) systems, which showed that the effect of a heatwave on parasite traits depended on the amplitude of the extreme event.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schreven et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: According to the temperature variability hypothesis, parasites should acclimatise more rapidly to changing temperatures than their larger hosts due to their faster metabolic rates from smaller size.
source: According to the temperature variability hypothesis (Raffel et al., 2012; Rohr et al., 2013), parasites, which have faster metabolic rates due to their smaller size, should acclimatise more rapidly to changing temperatures than their larger hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raffel et al., 2012 and Rohr et al., 2013.

claim: Host resistance may decrease as a result of the trade-off between the energy demand for acclimatization and immunity.
source: Moreover, host resistance may also decrease as a result of the trade-off between the energy demand for acclimatization and immunity (Nelson and Demas, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nelson and Demas, 1996.

claim: Varying temperature can lead to higher infection prevalence in Cuban tree frogs, red-spotted newts, and abalone.
source: That varying temperature can lead to higher infection prevalence has been established in Cuban tree frogs, red-spotted newts, and abalone (Ben-Horin et al., 2013; Raffel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ben-Horin et al., 2013 and Raffel et al., 2012.

claim: Growth rates of Ordospora increase by a factor of 5 between 20°C and 24°C before declining again.
source: Estimates show that growth rates of Ordospora increase by a factor of 5 between 20°C and 24°C before declining again (Kirk et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2018.

claim: A reduction in reproductive output of the host under variable temperatures is consistent with previous work on Daphnia.
source: A reduction in reproductive output of the host under variable temperatures is consistent with previous work both on Daphnia (Schwartz et al., 2016) and in other systems (Craig and Kipling, 1983; Uvarov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2016.

claim: A reduction in reproductive output of the host under variable temperatures is consistent with previous work in other systems.
source: A reduction in reproductive output of the host under variable temperatures is consistent with previous work both on Daphnia (Schwartz et al., 2016) and in other systems (Craig and Kipling, 1983; Uvarov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Craig and Kipling, 1983 and Uvarov et al., 2011.

claim: A reduction in host fecundity due to parasitism is well established.
source: Similarly, a reduction in host fecundity due to parasitism is well established (Ebert, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert, 2005.

claim: Infection may reduce the thermal tolerance of the host.
source: Infection may also reduce the thermal tolerance of the host (Hector et al., 2019), which would explain the small shift of the thermal optimum for host reproduction under the heatwave regime.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hector et al., 2019.

claim: Extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to disease-driven collapses of keystone predators.
source: Indeed, extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to disease-driven collapses of keystone predators (Harvell et al., 2019), increases in diseases such as dengue and cholera (Anyamba et al., 2019), and shifts in the geographic distribution of pathogens (Claar and Wood, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harvell et al., 2019.

claim: Extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to increases in diseases such as dengue and cholera.
source: Indeed, extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to disease-driven collapses of keystone predators (Harvell et al., 2019), increases in diseases such as dengue and cholera (Anyamba et al., 2019), and shifts in the geographic distribution of pathogens (Claar and Wood, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anyamba et al., 2019.

claim: Extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to shifts in the geographic distribution of pathogens.
source: Indeed, extreme temperature events such as El Niño have been linked to disease-driven collapses of keystone predators (Harvell et al., 2019), increases in diseases such as dengue and cholera (Anyamba et al., 2019), and shifts in the geographic distribution of pathogens (Claar and Wood, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Claar and Wood, 2020.

claim: Daphnia are filter feeders that consume planktonic algae and other microorganisms.
source: Daphnia are filter feeders that consume planktonic algae and other microorganisms, thus promoting water transparency and helping to prevent algal blooms (Miner et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miner et al., 2012.

claim: Daphnia promote water transparency and help to prevent algal blooms.
source: Daphnia are filter feeders that consume planktonic algae and other microorganisms, thus promoting water transparency and helping to prevent algal blooms (Miner et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miner et al., 2012.

claim: Daphnia are a key food source for planktivorous fish.
source: They are a key food source for planktivorous fish, constitute a major part in the food web (Ebert, 2005), and play a key role in nutrient cycling (Elser et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert, 2005.

claim: Daphnia constitute a major part in the food web.
source: They are a key food source for planktivorous fish, constitute a major part in the food web (Ebert, 2005), and play a key role in nutrient cycling (Elser et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert, 2005.

claim: Daphnia play a key role in nutrient cycling.
source: They are a key food source for planktivorous fish, constitute a major part in the food web (Ebert, 2005), and play a key role in nutrient cycling (Elser et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elser et al., 2000.

claim: O. colligata is a widely distributed microsporidium parasite that is only known to infect D. magna.
source: Here, we use O. colligata, a widely distributed microsporidium parasite that is only known to infect D. magna.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the study system.

claim: O. colligata has been recently used as a model to understand how changes in mean temperatures under global warming may affect host-parasite systems.
source: This gut parasite has been recently used as a model to understand how changes in mean temperatures under global warming may affect host-parasite systems (Kirk et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2020.

claim: Daphnia become infected when they accidentally ingest water borne spores of Ordospora while filter feeding.
source: Daphnia become infected when they accidentally ingest water borne spores of Ordospora while filter feeding.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the infection mechanism.

claim: After successful establishment, Ordospora spores divide intracellularly in the gut epithelium of D. magna.
source: After successful establishment, spores divide intracellularly in the gut epithelium of D. magna (Larsson et al., 1997) until they form a cluster of 32–64 spores.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larsson et al., 1997.

claim: Ordospora spores form clusters of 32–64 spores.
source: After successful establishment, spores divide intracellularly in the gut epithelium of D. magna (Larsson et al., 1997) until they form a cluster of 32–64 spores.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larsson et al., 1997.

claim: Ordospora spores are released either to the environment or go on to infecting neighboring cells after O. colligata lyses the cell.
source: Spores are then released either to the environment or go on to infecting neighboring cells after O. colligata lyses the cell.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the parasite's life cycle.

claim: The Beta Function provides realistic predictions when extrapolating beyond the measured thermal range.
source: While there are numerous non-linear functions that can be used to fit thermal performance curves (e.g., Briére, Ratkowsky equation), the advantage of using the Beta Function is that it provides realistic predictions when extrapolating beyond the measured thermal range and that each of its parameters has a clear a biological meaning (see Shi et al., 2016, for a comparison of thermal performance equations), where Fm is the fitness at optimal performance for the fitted host or parasite trait, Topt is the temperature at optimal performance, and Tmin and Tmax are, respectively, the critical minimum and maximum temperatures over which fitness of the trait becomes unviable.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2016.

claim: Each parameter of the Beta Function has a clear biological meaning.
source: While there are numerous non-linear functions that can be used to fit thermal performance curves (e.g., Briére, Ratkowsky equation), the advantage of using the Beta Function is that it provides realistic predictions when extrapolating beyond the measured thermal range and that each of its parameters has a clear a biological meaning (see Shi et al., 2016, for a comparison of thermal performance equations), where Fm is the fitness at optimal performance for the fitted host or parasite trait, Topt is the temperature at optimal performance, and Tmin and Tmax are, respectively, the critical minimum and maximum temperatures over which fitness of the trait becomes unviable.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2016.

claim: The Beta Function has been shown to capture thermal performance accurately.
source: This non-linear function has been shown to capture thermal performance accurately (Niehaus et al., 2012) and has the advantage that all four parameters in the equation have clear biological meaning.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2012.

claim: No infection occurs in the Daphnia-Ordospora system below 12°C.
source: We chose these temperature levels because of their relevance for our host and pathogen system, as no infection occurs below 12°C and hosts have high mortality above 30°C (Kirk et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirk et al., 2018 and Kirk et al., 2019.

claim: Daphnia hosts have high mortality above 30°C.
source: We chose these temperature levels because of their relevance for our host and pathogen system, as no infection occurs below 12°C and hosts have high mortality above 30°C (Kirk et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirk et al., 2018 and Kirk et al., 2019.

claim: The variable temperature regimes mimic naturally occurring temperature events in small ponds and rock pools.
source: These variable temperature regimes were selected to mimic naturally occurring temperature events in habitats our study organisms encounter naturally (i.e., small ponds and rock pools) (Jacobs et al., 2008; Kuha et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2008 and Kuha et al., 2018.

claim: Constant temperature regimes were replicated 12 times.
source: Constant temperature regimes were replicated 12 times (7×12×2=168 individuals), while in the variable temperature regimes, the number of replicates was increased to 18 as we expected increased mortality in these treatments (5×18×2=180 and 4×18×2=144, respectively, for the fluctuating and heatwave regime).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Variable temperature regimes had 18 replicates.
source: Constant temperature regimes were replicated 12 times (7×12×2=168 individuals), while in the variable temperature regimes, the number of replicates was increased to 18 as we expected increased mortality in these treatments (5×18×2=180 and 4×18×2=144, respectively, for the fluctuating and heatwave regime).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: All animals were terminated after day 27 and fitness estimates were collected within 3 days.
source: All animals were terminated after day 27 and fitness estimates were collected within 3 days.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The thermal stress hypothesis suggests that a shift in temperature may reduce the performance of either host or parasite.
source: Though Ordospora should have an overall advantage under the temperature variability hypothesis, the realized advantage may be smaller as its thermal range is more restricted than its host (Kirk et al., 2018). The heatwave may thus cause proportionally more stress in the parasite than the host at high temperatures, consistent with the thermal stress hypothesis, which suggests that a shift in temperature may reduce the performance of either host or parasite (Paull et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paull et al., 2015.

claim: Thermal stress can affect host and pathogen performance.
source: Indeed, that thermal stress can affect host and pathogen performance has been well supported (Gehman et al., 2018; Kirk et al., 2019; Schreven et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gehman et al., 2018, Kirk et al., 2019, Schreven et al., 2017, and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: The thermal range of Ordospora is more restricted than its host.
source: Though Ordospora should have an overall advantage under the temperature variability hypothesis, the realized advantage may be smaller as its thermal range is more restricted than its host (Kirk et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2018.

claim: The optimal performance of Ordospora occurs around 19°C.
source: While the optimal performance of Ordospora occurs around 19°C, due to the balance of thermal performance curves of other host and pathogen traits (e.g., mortality, infectivity, etc.), a temporary increase to 22°C, as occurred under our heatwave at 16°C, may thus have exacerbated pathogen growth, particularly if different traits react differently to a temperature disturbance, which may have disrupted the balance between host and parasite.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Average infection rates under diurnal temperature fluctuations would be expected to be lower due to the non-linear nature of the thermal performance curve (Jensen's inequality).
source: As filtration rates of D. magna decline at higher temperatures (Kirk et al., 2019), average infection rates under diurnal temperature fluctuations would also be expected to be lower due to the non-linear nature of the thermal performance curve (i.e., Jensen's inequality; Dowd et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dowd et al., 2015.

claim: The effect of the heatwave on established infections may have been limited because the heatwave occurred 20 days post-infection.
source: However, given that our heatwave occurred 20 days post-infection and that Daphnia are not known to recover from infection (Ebert, 2005), the effect of the heatwave on established infections may have been limited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of the heatwave and the citation to Ebert, 2005.

claim: Changing patterns of climate variation, superimposed on shifts in mean temperatures due to global warming, may have profound and unanticipated effects on disease dynamics.
source: We conclude that changing patterns of climate variation, superimposed on shifts in mean temperatures due to global warming, may have profound and unanticipated effects on disease dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance can be highly complex.
source: Our results demonstrate that the combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance can be highly complex, and may alter the vulnerability of host populations (Harvell et al., 2019), affect the evolution of host and parasites (Buckley and Huey, 2016), and, therefore, impede our ability to accurately predict future disease outbreaks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with supporting citations.

claim: The combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance may alter the vulnerability of host populations.
source: Our results demonstrate that the combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance can be highly complex, and may alter the vulnerability of host populations (Harvell et al., 2019), affect the evolution of host and parasites (Buckley and Huey, 2016), and, therefore, impede our ability to accurately predict future disease outbreaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harvell et al., 2019.

claim: The combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance may affect the evolution of host and parasites.
source: Our results demonstrate that the combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance can be highly complex, and may alter the vulnerability of host populations (Harvell et al., 2019), affect the evolution of host and parasites (Buckley and Huey, 2016), and, therefore, impede our ability to accurately predict future disease outbreaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buckley and Huey, 2016.

claim: The combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance may impede our ability to accurately predict future disease outbreaks.
source: Our results demonstrate that the combined effect of changing temperature mean and variance can be highly complex, and may alter the vulnerability of host populations (Harvell et al., 2019), affect the evolution of host and parasites (Buckley and Huey, 2016), and, therefore, impede our ability to accurately predict future disease outbreaks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and supporting citations.

claim: Temperature variation can affect disease dynamics in human, wildlife, and livestock populations with potentially devastating economic and health consequences.
source: While temperature variation can thus affect disease dynamics in human, wildlife, and livestock populations—with potentially devastating economic and health consequences (Altizer et al., 2013)—the complexity of the effects of temperature and its variation currently limits our ability to move beyond system-specific predictions, in particular for extreme temperature events (Claar and Wood, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Altizer et al., 2013.

claim: The complexity of the effects of temperature and its variation currently limits our ability to move beyond system-specific predictions, in particular for extreme temperature events.
source: While temperature variation can thus affect disease dynamics in human, wildlife, and livestock populations—with potentially devastating economic and health consequences (Altizer et al., 2013)—the complexity of the effects of temperature and its variation currently limits our ability to move beyond system-specific predictions, in particular for extreme temperature events (Claar and Wood, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Claar and Wood, 2020.

claim: Altered patterns of temperature variance lead to an almost order-of-magnitude shift in thermal performance of host and pathogen life-history traits over and above the effects of mean temperature.
source: Here, we show that altered patterns of temperature variance lead to an almost order-of-magnitude shift in thermal performance of host and pathogen life-history traits over and above the effects of mean temperature and, moreover, that different temperature regimes affect these traits differently.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Different temperature regimes affect host and pathogen life-history traits differently.
source: Here, we show that altered patterns of temperature variance lead to an almost order-of-magnitude shift in thermal performance of host and pathogen life-history traits over and above the effects of mean temperature and, moreover, that different temperature regimes affect these traits differently.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The host response to the variable temperature regimes differed from that of the pathogen.
source: The host response to the variable temperature regimes differed from that of the pathogen (compare thermal performance curves for the heatwave and diurnal fluctuating regimes between Figure 2A and B & C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: While host performance was reduced under both variable temperature regimes, parasite traits showed either a narrowing of the performance curve or no effect and greatly increased performance.
source: While host performance was reduced (lower Fm) under both variable temperature regimes, parasite traits showed either a narrowing of the performance curve (for diurnal fluctuations) or no effect and greatly increased performance (for infection and burden under the heatwave).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Not only does temperature variation alter the thermal performance of host and pathogen life-history traits in a unique way, but the type of variation and the mean temperature at which it occurs are also critical.
source: We show that, not only does temperature variation alter the thermal performance of host and pathogen life-history traits in a unique way—driving a shift in performance up to order-of-magnitude over and above the effect of mean temperature—but that the type of variation and the mean temperature at which it occurs are also critical.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion directly stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: Each of the life-history traits measured was affected differently by thermal variation.
source: Indeed, each of the life-history traits we measured was affected differently by thermal variation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: Spore burden was nearly identical for all three temperature regimes at ~19°C.
source: However, while spore burden was different at ~16°C, spore burden at ~19°C was nearly identical for all three temperature regimes.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spore burdens of both constant and fluctuating temperature regimes were similar near the optimum temperature of 19°C.
source: This is supported further by the consistently lower spore burden for the fluctuating regime when compared with the constant temperature regime except near the optimum temperature of 19°C, where spore burdens of both temperature regimes were similar (confidence intervals for Topt and Fm overlap).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The heatwave did not differ from the fluctuating regime for infection rates, as estimates for the maximum temperature had broad confidence intervals.
source: However, unlike the constant temperature regime, the heatwave did not differ from the fluctuating regime, as estimates for the maximum temperature had broad confidence intervals, likely caused by lack of data at the higher temperatures.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lack of data at high temperatures likely caused broad confidence intervals for the heatwave's maximum temperature estimates.
source: However, unlike the constant temperature regime, the heatwave did not differ from the fluctuating regime, as estimates for the maximum temperature had broad confidence intervals, likely caused by lack of data at the higher temperatures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data limitations.

claim: Extrapolations of results beyond the highest heatwave temperature should be interpreted with caution.
source: Our estimates of maximum temperature for the heatwave, however, have broad confidence intervals, likely due to the lack of data at high temperatures, and extrapolations of our results beyond our highest heatwave temperature (which was 22°C and reached 28°C during the 3-day heatwave which was close to the estimated maximum thermal tolerance of the parasite) should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on data limitations.

claim: The highest heatwave temperature was 22°C and reached 28°C during the 3-day heatwave.
source: Our estimates of maximum temperature for the heatwave, however, have broad confidence intervals, likely due to the lack of data at high temperatures, and extrapolations of our results beyond our highest heatwave temperature (which was 22°C and reached 28°C during the 3-day heatwave which was close to the estimated maximum thermal tolerance of the parasite) should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: 28°C during the 3-day heatwave was close to the estimated maximum thermal tolerance of the parasite.
source: Our estimates of maximum temperature for the heatwave, however, have broad confidence intervals, likely due to the lack of data at high temperatures, and extrapolations of our results beyond our highest heatwave temperature (which was 22°C and reached 28°C during the 3-day heatwave which was close to the estimated maximum thermal tolerance of the parasite) should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.
